newsitem.title: USA: LME still lacks teeth to tackle fraud - Threlkeld.
newsitem.headline: LME still lacks teeth to tackle fraud - Threlkeld.

text.p: Tighter regulation of the London Metal Exchange as recommended in Thursday's Securities and Investments Board review still fails to give the London exchange real powers to tackle corruption, trader David Threlkeld said.
"The SIB is not confronting the real issue of the Sumitomo affair, and the real issue is that someone was involved in massive fraud and manipulation," Threlkeld said.
Despite the U.K. regulatory watchdog's recommendations, there were still "no mechanics" to deal with fraud in the market, leaving the exchange open to future fraud, he added.
"The LME has not been given teeth to bite," Threlkeld said. "My own position is that you need a new executive entity on the LME with teeth and powers to put a stop to corruption and fraud."
Threlkeld alerted the LME in the early 1990s that former Sumitomo Corp star trader Yasuo Hamanaka had asked him to provide records for ficticious trades done between them.
In June Sumitomo announced it had sacked Hamanaka for notching up multi-billion dollar losses from unauthorised copper trades.
The LME called on the SIB to review how the exchange operated as criticism of the London exchange mounted amid market turmoil.
But Threlkeld appeared to be a lone voice among U.S. based traders who generally breathed a sigh of relief there will be no big shake-up of the world's biggest base metals market.
Not that anyone expected major reforms.

"A lot of the problems related to Sumitomo were not part of the LME marketplace," said Mike Frawley of Dean Witter Reynolds. "The marketplace functions well and we cannot police the internal operations of non-members.
A broker at an LME ring dealing member added, "A lot of people are happy with the system. Criticism from the U.S. has been the only impetus for change."
"If the LME was more like U.S. exchanges, it would not be as beneficial," the broker added.
A key critic of LME was rival New York Mercantile Exchange (NYMEX), whose COMEX division also trades copper futures and options. NYMEX officials were not immediately available for comment.
A merchant said the SIB report was just a "slap on the wrist", but said no fundamental changes to LME were needed.
"The LME is a pretty successful system and I don't honestly know what they could do unless they go the complete American way and everyone reports everything all the time."
Daily reporting of LME stocks, as suggested in the SIB review, would not be beneficial and could confuse the market, he said. At present the LME reports stocks twice a week.

"It's probably even better to do it twice a week. If you are trading basis 5,000-tonne moves in stocks, it's probably not the best way to go anyway. I think more happens on the belief of what stocks should be than on the actual result," the merchant said.
